opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the places where I think people underestimate how much the bootstrapping matters. If you start AlphaZero-style from a completely random network, the value function is basically noise at first. Self-play games between two random players end in pretty arbitrary outcomes, so your value targets are extremely high-variance, and it can take a lot of compute before the signal sharpens up.

My practical recommendation is to not be a purist about it. If you have access to human game records, and for Go there are millions of professional and strong amateur games out there, do a supervised pretraining phase first. Train the policy head to predict the next move, and train the value head to predict the eventual game outcome from each position. That's essentially what the original AlphaGo did, and it gets you a network that already has a reasonable sense of what good shape looks like and who's ahead.

There's a subtlety with the value head, though. If you train it naively on every position from human games, it overfits badly, because positions within a single game are highly correlated. They share the same outcome label and look almost identical move to move. So the network memorizes games instead of learning to evaluate positions. The fix, which DeepMind also used, is to sample only one or a few positions per game, so you get many more independent outcomes relative to the number of training examples.

Another trick is to use cheap signals that correlate with winning. In Go you can do a quick score estimate, territory counting, or even use the final ownership map of each intersection as an auxiliary target. KataGo did a lot of this, predicting ownership and score margin in addition to win/loss. Those auxiliary heads give much denser supervision than a single bit at the end of the game, so the network's representation learns faster, and the value head benefits from that.

And if you don't have human data, or you deliberately want to avoid it, you can curriculum your way up: start on smaller boards like 9x9, where games are short and the credit assignment problem is much easier, get a decent value function there, and then transfer to 19x19. Convolutional nets transfer across board sizes surprisingly well since the local patterns are similar.

So, in short: pretrain on human games if you can, sample positions sparsely to avoid overfitting the value head, add dense auxiliary targets like ownership and score, and if you're starting from scratch, use smaller boards as a curriculum. Each of these reduces how long you spend in that early regime where self-play is just generating noise.

r001.rationale: Recommends supervised pretraining on human Go records and training the value head to predict game outcomes before self-play.

r002.rationale: Describes random self-play as noisy and high variance; it does not say that random self-play on a small board produces sufficient data for a good value function.

r003.rationale: Recommends learning on 9×9 and transferring to 19×19, but does not state that training on data from both board sizes enables the transfer.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that you mostly don't need a good initial value function, and trying too hard to get one is a bit of a trap. The thing that makes self-play work in Go is that the search is doing a lot of the heavy lifting. Even a value function that's basically noise at the start gets corrected by MCTS, because the tree search is looking several moves ahead and the game has a clean terminal signal. You win or you lose, and that signal propagates back through all the positions you visited.

So what AlphaZero did, which I think is the right default, is just start from random weights and let the search bootstrap the value. The early games look terrible, the networks are confidently wrong about everything, but the win-loss labels at the end of each game are ground truth, and you regress onto those. Within a surprisingly small number of iterations the value estimates become meaningful, and then the search gets better, which makes the training data better, and you get this flywheel.

If you want to shortcut the first phase, there are a couple of things that help. One is just training on human games first, the way the original AlphaGo did with the supervised policy network. That gives you a decent prior over which moves are even worth expanding, which makes the early search way more sample efficient. The downside is you inherit human biases, and the system has to unlearn some of them later. The other trick is to start with a simpler proxy for value, like a territory count or a rollout-based estimate using a fast policy, and use that as a warm start. You don't keep it, you just use it to make the first few thousand games less random.

But I'd push back on the framing a little. The thing people usually get wrong isn't the initial value function, it's the training signal. If you're using the final game outcome as your target, your value function is going to be very noisy early on because the outcomes are driven by random blunders. A lot of the practical wins come from targets that are less noisy, like regressing onto the search's own value estimate at each node rather than the raw game result, or mixing the two. That's a much bigger lever than how you initialize.

And the other thing I'd say, coming at this from the robotics side, is that Go is kind of the easy case for this. You have a perfect simulator, a dense terminal reward, and unlimited free data. The reason initialization matters so much more in robotics is that none of those are true. You can't just play a million games against yourself, so you can't afford to start from noise. In Go you can, so you should.

r001.rationale: The response mentions human games to initialize a supervised policy network and a proxy value warm start, but does not recommend expert Go data to initialize the value function.

r002.rationale: It says random weights can bootstrap through self-play, but does not specify a small Go board or say that data from one is sufficient to learn a good value function.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention training on both 9×9 and 19×19 data or transferring a value function between those board sizes.

astra-6.text:
I’d bootstrap it from a policy that plays reasonably well. You can train a policy on human games, use it to play games out to completion, and then train the value function to predict who wins from intermediate positions. That gives you an initial estimate of how good a position is under that policy. Then you use the value function to improve play through search, generate better self-play games, and repeat.

You can also start entirely from random play, because Go gives you a clear win-or-loss signal at the end. But then you’re learning the policy and the value function together from a much weaker starting point.

r001.rationale: Recommends training a policy on human games, then using its completed games to train an initial value function before self-play improvement.

r002.rationale: Mentions starting from random play, but does not say that random self-play on a small board produces enough data to learn a good value function.

r003.rationale: Does not mention training on 9×9 and 19×19 data or transferring a value function between board sizes.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d bootstrap it from the outcomes of games. You don’t need a good value function to start—you can initialize the network randomly, have it play against itself, and train it to predict who eventually wins from each position. Those predictions will be pretty crude initially, but they give your search something to work with. As search improves the quality of the games, you get better training data, and that feedback loop improves both the policy and the value function.

If you want a head start, you can also train on human games. But the interesting thing about self-play is that you can build the value function from the rules and the final win-or-loss signal.

r001.rationale: It says human games can provide a head start, but does not specify expert Go data or clearly recommend it as the initialization before self-play.

r002.rationale: It describes random initialization followed by self-play training, but does not mention a small Go board or say that this data is sufficient to learn a good value function.

r003.rationale: It does not mention training on both 9×9 and 19×19 data or transferring a value function between those board sizes.
